items.name: First screen
items.reason: From the headline, decision block and lead claim (only_survivor), a reader learns what to do: route with Brisk-S few-shot. They learn why: it is the only configuration of nine that passes the balanced-accuracy gate, every cell floor and the latency budget. They also learn the main risk: a 0.7-point clearance on 90.7% against 90%, plus Complex × News at 82.9%. The options check agrees that this arm is the sole survivor and the dominant option.

items.name: Coherent story
items.reason: The claims build on each other. only_survivor gives the sole survivor. news_column shows where it is thinnest (Complex × News at 82.9%, interval 81.7–84.1%). nano_gap shows that this cell separates it from Nano-XS few-shot (+6.2, +4.4 to +8). I found no row in any values table that contradicts its sentence. The gate table, cell table and the sweeps in 'What you could change' match the threshold checks: Nano-XS few-shot becomes the pick at a floor of 76.7% or lower, and nothing passes above 82.9% or below 184 ms.

items.name: Honest emphasis
items.reason: The pick's weak points are on the first screen: a 0.7-point gate clearance, Complex × News as the thinnest cell, and a latency clearance with no spread. But the confidence line reads high over the latency caveat without saying why the 66 ms clearance should hold. The lede and nano_gap also frame Nano-XS few-shot as 'a fraction of the cost' ($1,143 a month, 21 times) without saying that these costs come from provider routing the input never names.

items.name: Sound elision
items.reason: Nothing omitted would change the decision. Macro F1 and traffic-weighted accuracy order the arms as balanced accuracy does. Every Atlas-M arm misses latency by at least 170 ms. Every other excluded arm fails a gate already shown, and the options check confirms this. Cost does not move a decision that has one survivor.

items.name: Confounds handled
items.reason: No control, and no production router run beside the arms: the page carries this and reads against gate lines, so it is handled. The unnamed provider and serving stack is not handled well enough. The method section says so, but nano_gap's cost gap and the p95 latency both depend on how each model was served. The body states both figures as properties of the models, and only the fourth next step touches the provider.

items.name: Actionable next steps
items.reason: Each step names a run and what it settles. The fresh run of at least 19,383 cases matches the two-sided four-in-five sizing for the 0.7-point clearance. The Nano-XS news step names the 3.3-point gap to the floor and the 26.5% chance that its overall clearance reads the wrong way. The repeated latency runs on the serving stack size the 66 ms clearance. The declaration step covers the volume unit and the providers.

items.name: Evidence fits claims
items.reason: only_survivor's scatter and news_column's heatmap fit their claims, and both would flip if their values flipped. nano_gap's caption says the block shows 'overall and in each place', but it has no overall row, and one bound prints as -0.03699. prompt_lever's sentence sets +11.9 (Nano-XS, zero-shot to few-shot) against +0.8 (Brisk-S, few-shot to rubric). Those are different moves, so they don't support 'worked examples matter most for the smallest model'. The matching contrast, +4.7 for Brisk-S zero-shot to few-shot, is in the same block.

findings.finding: nano_gap compares cost by model without naming who served each one: Brisk-S few-shot 'costs $1,143 a month more' than Nano-XS few-shot. The lede ('at a fraction of the cost') and the second next step ('costs 21 times as much as') do the same. The input states no provider or pricing for either arm, and the method section admits the routing is unknown. A cost belongs to the provider routing, not the model. Fix: in nano_gap's sentence, and wherever the 21× or $1,143 appears, say these are the costs as this run served each model, with the provider unknown, so the gap may not hold under another routing.

The confidence line reads high over three open caveats, and the latency clause does not stand behind its own. It says the call fails 'only if the p95 latency moves from run to run by as much as its 66 ms clearance', but not why the call should hold until that is measured. The serving stack behind the 184 ms p95 is never named, so production could plausibly read differently. The selection clause is also garbled ('The pick is the best of several candidates. only if…'), and its '0.0004972%' is false precision for a figure the page then says selection moves by an unknown amount. Fix: limit the high to the accuracy and cell-floor findings, whose intervals clear their lines, and say the latency pass is unsized until the repeated-run step reports. Either give a reason the 66 ms (about a quarter of the budget) should hold, or lower the confidence form.

prompt_lever's sentence contrasts different moves: +11.9 is Nano-XS going from zero-shot to few-shot, while +0.8 is Brisk-S going from few-shot to rubric + reasoning. To show that worked examples matter most for the smallest model, compare +11.9 with Brisk-S zero-shot to few-shot (+4.7, +4.2 to +5.2), or cite the interaction row (+7.2, +6.5 to +7.9). Both are already in the block.

nano_gap's caption says each row is the difference 'overall and in each place both hold it', but the block has no overall row. Add the overall row, Brisk-S few-shot less Nano-XS few-shot on balanced accuracy: +0.6, interval +0.2 to +1.0 (the flip of prompt_lever's -0.6, -1.0 to -0.2). Or drop 'overall' from the caption. Round the Simple × Science bound (-0.03699) to -0.04. The sentence 'what that buys is news' overstates the case: Simple × News leans the other way (-0.5) and Medium × News is +1.5. Say 'chiefly Complex × News'.

One gate goes by two names. Watch and the gate table call it 'Overall accuracy', while the headline, recommendation and method call it the balanced-accuracy gate. A reader could take 'overall accuracy' to mean traffic-weighted accuracy (92.2% for the pick), which would make the 0.7-point margin look like 2.2. Use 'balanced accuracy' everywhere the gate is named.

In 'What you could change', the latency row says that when the budget is loosened, slower options enter 'but each costs more, and the pick holds'. Above 496 ms, Brisk-S rubric (91.5%) and Atlas-M few-shot (92.1%) would pass every gate with higher balanced accuracy, so the pick would then rest on cost. The page says elsewhere that cost decides nothing and that its routing is unknown. Say the pick holds only if the lower cost is preferred to 0.8–1.4 more points of balanced accuracy.

The Watch line names the main risks: a 0.7-point clearance on an option picked as the best of nine, the Complex × News cell at 82.9%, and a latency pass with no interval. The high is now limited to the accuracy and cell-floor findings, the latency pass is scoped out until the repeated-run step reports, and the garbled selection clause and its false-precision 0.0004972% are gone.

items.name: Coherent story

In nano_gap, the overall gap is +0.6 (+0.2 to +1) and Complex × News is +6.2 (+4.4 to +8), while the Simple cells lean the other way. items.reason: The pick's weak axes are visible: the thin balanced-accuracy clearance, the thinnest cell and the latency pass with no interval. The latency row in 'What you could change' now says that above 483–496 ms the pick holds only if its lower cost is preferred to 0.8–1.4 more points, which resolves my earlier finding. One small overstatement remains in the cell-floor row (see findings): Nano-XS few-shot is said to 'become the pick' even though its balanced accuracy only borderline clears the gate.

items.name: Evidence fits claims
items.reason: My earlier nano_gap finding is mostly resolved. The block now carries the overall row its caption promises, and the sentence says 'chiefly from Complex × News'. Each block shows its claim's figure, and its values would change the claim if they flipped. One leftover: the Simple × Science lower bound is still printed as -0.03699.

findings.finding: In 'What you could change', the cell-floor row says that at a floor of 76.7% or below, Nano-XS few-shot 'becomes the pick'. The lede says the call would change if Nano-XS few-shot lifted Complex × News above the floor. Both leave out two conditions. First, Nano-XS few-shot's balanced accuracy of 90.1% only borderline clears the 90% gate: settle_cases puts the distance at +0.1, and this design would read it on the wrong side 26.5% of the time. Second, it would replace Brisk-S few-shot only on cost, as this run's unnamed routing served it. Fix: in both places, say Nano-XS few-shot would take over only if it also holds the balanced-accuracy gate on a re-run, and only on cost as this run served it. The third next step already says this, so it only needs carrying up.
This is left over from my earlier finding. The cell block still prints the Simple × Science lower bound as -0.03699. Round it to -0.04 to match the other bounds.

items.name: First screen
items.reason: The headline and decision block say what to do: route turns with Brisk-S few-shot, the only one of nine options that passes the balanced-accuracy gate, every cell floor and the latency budget. They also give the reason, and Watch names the main risk: a 0.7-point clearance on an option picked from nine, and an unsized 66 ms latency clearance. The lead claim (only_survivor) and its scatter confirm it. options_dominance with gates applied gives Brisk-S few-shot as the only survivor. My earlier finding is fixed: the lede now says Nano-XS few-shot would replace the pick only on cost as this run served it, and only if it also holds the balanced-accuracy gate on a re-run.

items.name: Coherent story
items.reason: I checked each claim against its table row by row. In news_column, News is the lowest column in every row for both few-shot models, and Complex × News for Brisk-S few-shot is 82.9% (81.7–84.1). In nano_gap, the +0.6 (+0.2 to +1) matches compare.brisk-s.few.nano-xs.few.balanced_accuracy.overall. Complex × News at +6.2 accounts for the whole gap once divided across nine cells, and the other cells are small or favour Nano-XS. In prompt_lever, the +11.9, +4.7 and +0.8 rows match. The 'What you could change' rows match decision_sensitivity. The cell-floor sweep flips at 76.7% (Nano-XS few-shot) and at 82.9%. The latency sweep never changes the cost-weighted call, which agrees with the page saying a looser budget changes the pick only if you prefer accuracy to cost.

items.name: Honest emphasis
items.reason: The pick's weak axes are in plain view. The balanced-accuracy clearance is 0.7 points on a best-of-nine pick. Complex × News is 2.9 points over the floor. The latency pass has no interval, and the confidence block explicitly leaves it out of the high. The cost advantage over Atlas-M and the cost gap to Nano-XS are both tied to this run's unnamed routing. Nothing claims more than its interval supports. Brisk-S few-shot would land on the wrong side of the gate in 0.0005% of runs (settle.criteria.overall.brisk-s.few.overall.wrong_side), so 'clears with its whole interval' is fair.

items.name: Sound elision
items.reason: None of the omissions changes the decision. Macro F1 and traffic-weighted accuracy order the options as balanced accuracy does, and the appendix holds them. The Atlas-M cells can't matter because every Atlas-M prompt misses latency, and the latency row in 'What you could change' covers the case where the budget loosens. My earlier rounding finding on the Simple × Science bound (-0.03699): the analyst explains the renderer prints the figure as the data hold it, and the caption now says the bound sits just below zero. I accept that and have logged the formatting as a tool gap rather than re-raising it.

items.name: Confounds handled
items.reason: The unnamed provider and serving stack is carried on only_survivor and nano_gap, scoped in the confidence block (accuracy findings don't depend on it, latency and cost do), and covered by next steps 2 and 4. Best-of-nine selection gets a re-run sized at 19,383 cases, which matches the two-sided four-in-five size from settle_cases. The latency point estimate gets repeated p95 runs. The missing control is scoped to comparisons between options, which the call doesn't rest on. The cost_served_by fact is addressed: every cost comparison says providers are unnamed and that another routing could change the gap. The high_over_open fact is addressed too: each of the four caveats says what would make it matter, and the high is explicitly limited to the accuracy and cell-floor findings.

items.name: Actionable next steps
items.reason: Each step names an experiment or a declaration and what it settles. Step 1: a fresh run of at least 19,383 cases settles whether the 0.7-point clearance survives selection. Step 2: repeated p95 runs on the production stack size the 66 ms clearance. Step 3: news examples for Nano-XS few-shot need a 3.3-point gain in Complex × News, plus a re-read of the overall set, since its 90.1% balanced accuracy reads on the wrong side 26.5% of the time. Step 4 declares the volume unit and providers behind the cost figures.

items.name: Evidence fits claims
items.reason: Each block carries its claim's own figure, and every number I spot-checked matches the tool: monthly cost $1,200, gap +$1,143, 21×, 26.5%, 19,383, and interval half-widths of 1.4 and 1.2. The gate scatter shows both gates and its caption flags that Nano-XS few-shot also lands in the box but misses a cell floor. The next claim's heatmap shows that miss with its interval. nano_gap shows the gap itself, overall and per cell, with unpaired intervals. Each counterfactual holds: if Complex × News for Nano-XS few-shot were above 80%, or the pick's lower bound fell below 90%, the claims would have to change.
